catalog_quote: There is a default stress rule in Yeri which places primary stress on the penultimate syllable. This stress rule is described in section 2.4.1. Although this is the most common location for primary stress to fall, it is not the only possible location. Section 2.4.2 describes an alternate stress pattern found in some trisyllabic words, while section 2.4.3 describes an uncommon stress pattern which places stress on the last syllable of specific disyllabic words. [p. 72] ... Primary stress in Yeri generally falls on the penultimate syllable of a lexical item with secondary stress on alternate syllables preceding the main stress. Vowel length is the primary acoustic correlate to stress and stressed vowels are phonetically longer than their unstressed counterparts. This can be quickly seen by considering the duration of each vowel in trisyllabic words like habaha /îabaîa/ [îa.m bá.îa] ‘habah…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the lexical word by default; secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables to the left of the primary (e.g. [mÒ.ni.kÉ.ta] 'water snake'). Stress is not contrastive. Prefixes, proclitics and augment allomorphs are not counted in the stress window (monosyllabic roots keep primary stress after prefixes, e.g. t1-wúl), whereas most suffixes are counted (agá-ki).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: 'secondary stress on alternate syllables preceding the main stress' (p. 73), marked with grave accents in quadrisyllables (Table 2.28); author notes a dispreference for stressing adjacent syllables giving 'rhythmic stress' (fn. 38, p. 81).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) An alternate pattern in some trisyllabic words with stress on antepenult and final syllable (primary location unclear), favoured when the penult is /i/, the final syllable has a coda or V+HV sequence, the antepenult is heavy with final /e/, or penult /e/ sits between obstruent and sonorant (sec. 2.4.2, Table 2.29). (b) A small class of disyllables with final codas or final /e/ shows variable penult/final stress (anór ~ ánor), explained historically by loss of word-final *a still present in Agi cognates (sec. 2.4.3). (c) Reduplicated words stress reduplicant and base equally (2.4.4). (d) Stress can shift leftward in connected speech, tied to rhythm, stress clash and speech rate (2.4.6). Author cautions (fn. 26) that much more research is needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word ('primary lexical stress' of a lexical item in isolation); the author explicitly separates this from sentential stress/stress shift in longer utterances (sec. 2.4.6). Vowel length is the main correlate; unstressed vowels reduce to [ɨ] or delete.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Yeri as spoken in Yapunda village (Sandaun/West Sepik, PNG); Glottolog names it Yapunda/Yeri (yapu1240, iso yev). No dialect split in the source. Wilson notes stress is not contrastive in Yeri, unlike Laycock's characterisation of Torricelli languages generally.
